Quotas and evidence | Constraint | Value | | --- | ---: | | Entries per browser workspace, including Trash | 1,000 | | Aggregate UTF-8 source, including retained Trash | 16 MiB | | Source per file | 32 KiB | | Deleted-content recovery | 48 hours | | Automatic expiry of active files | None | Trash counts toward quota until expired content is purged. Export important work before clearing browser data or reorganizing many folders. Workspace recovery is distinct from Ledger history: deleting an editable file does not rewrite immutable experiment evidence. See workspace API(../reference/workspace-api.md) for exact version semantics and backups(../operations/backup-recovery.md) for service-level disaster recovery.

title: Backup and recovery
text: Backup and recovery Mount durable storage for SQLite and snapshot it with a method that produces a consistent database copy. Retain multiple generations according to operational risk, encrypt backups, restrict access, and test restoration into a separate QORE instance. A backup that has never been restored is unverified. Explorer source also exists in browser storage. Database recovery does not restore cleared browser files, and browser source does not recreate missing immutable run evidence. Export important source before browser migration. Keep the public origin stable because cookies and browser storage are origin-scoped. Trash provides 48-hour application recovery for deleted workspace entries. It is not a disaster-recovery system and makes no promise about backup erasure schedules. Document which layer is being recovered before taking action.

title: Deployment guide
text: Deployment guide Build the frontend with the pinned pnpm lockfile, then build the root Dockerfile. Configure QORE_ENV=production, QORE_STORAGE=sqlite, the public HTTPS origin, and a QORE_DB_PATH inside a mounted persistent disk. Gemini configuration is optional and must be entered only in the host secret manager. After release, check health, create and refresh an Explorer file, run a small Bell or GHZ circuit, save a Ledger record, and verify QI both with and without attached source. Confirm that a second clean browser profile cannot list the first profile's records. Monitor memory during simulation and disk growth during repeated runs. Never use a successful image build as the only acceptance signal. Promotion requires backend tests, production acceptance, frontend build, browser contracts, security audit, and frontend audit. GitHub Actions should run the same reproducible baseline before main is deployed.

title: Scalability and capacity
text: Scalability and capacity QORE currently limits each API process to two concurrent quantum jobs and two concurrent Gemini calls. Budgets and queues are process-local. Horizontal replicas therefore require a shared rate limiter, durable job queue, centralized evidence store, and consistent browser-workspace routing before they represent one coherent service. Profile memory by circuit size and simulator method. Statevector cost grows exponentially with qubit count; the ten-qubit product limit is a correctness guard, not a complete capacity plan. Set host memory alerts, request latency metrics, worker timeout counts, provider error rates, and persistent-disk alerts. Static frontend assets can be cached aggressively because their names are content-hashed. API responses, workspace HTML, and private evidence use no-store/noindex behavior. Scale the static and compute paths independently only after preserving same-origin security and cookie semantics.

title: Security operations
text: Security operations QORE protects secrets by keeping provider credentials in the backend environment and excluding environment files, keys, certificates, databases, and credentials from Git. Frontend VITE_ variables are public bundle inputs and must never contain a provider key. The API applies trusted-host checks, same-origin write checks, request-size limits, strict schemas, constrained circuit parsing, per-workspace rate limits, worker concurrency, and secure response headers. Database lookups always combine an opaque browser scope with the requested identifier. This release has no verified user identity. An HttpOnly workspace cookie prevents casual cross-browser mixing but does not protect against another person controlling the same browser profile. Do not use the public deployment for confidential multi-tenant data. Add reviewed authentication, authorization, session revocation, and migration before that use case. Run scripts/security_checker.py --check before every release. If a credential was committed, remove it from the current tree, rotate or revoke it at the provider, inspect history and artifacts, and document the incident. Deleting one line does not revoke an already copied secret.

title: Verification and testing
text: Verification and testing Backend tests cover parsing, simulation, optimization, source hashing, immutable evidence, browser-workspace isolation, Trash, concurrency, origin policy, provider failure, and structured errors. Production acceptance executes real Qiskit/Aer cases rather than replacing numerical behavior with mocks. Frontend checks compile TypeScript, create the production bundle, and use Playwright to exercise onboarding, Explorer, QI, Lab, Forge, terminal, responsive layouts, and keyboard focus. Provider responses are mocked in UI contracts; that proves the interface contract, not live Gemini availability. A separate bounded provider probe verifies configuration without printing the key. The daily quality report combines security, frontend health, backend, and quantum stages. Keep the distinction between mocked evidence, real local computation, and external-service checks explicit. A red required stage blocks promotion.

title: QORE — PHASE 1 MVP
text: QORE — PHASE 1 MVP Complete Product, Engineering, Architecture & Design Specification Product: QORE Full identity: The Core of Quantum Development Category: Intelligent Development Environment for Quantum Software Core principle: AI proposes. Verification checks. Experiments provide the evidence. --- 1. Executive Summary QORE is an intelligent quantum software development environment designed to unify quantum programming, circuit visualization, simulation, optimization, verification, and reproducible experimentation. The goal is to make quantum software development more inspectable, measurable, and repeatable by connecting the entire development lifecycle within one coherent workspace. Instead of treating code editing, circuit visualization, simulation, optimization, and experiment tracking as isolated activities, QORE connects them through a shared quantum intermediate representation called QORE-IR. The platform follows an evidence-driven engineering philosophy: AI may propose changes, established quantum computing frameworks perform the actual computations, verification checks supported correctness properties, and experiment records preserve the evidence. Phase 1 establishes the foundation of this platform through a functional web-based IDE, a real local quantum simulator, a circuit analysis and optimization system, appropriate validation, and persistent experiment history. The objective is not to simulate the appearance of a complete quantum platform. It is to build a genuine, working foundation that can be extended into a broader quantum software infrastructure. 2. Product Vision and Problem Statement Quantum software development involves multiple connected tasks: - Writing quantum programs. - Translating source code into executable circuit representations. - Understanding gates, qubits, control relationships, and measurements. - Simulating quantum circuits. - Evaluating circuit complexity and resource requirements. - Optimizing circuit implementations. - Checking whether transformations preserve intended behavior. - Comparing theoretical expectations with measured outcomes. - Preserving the exact configurations and results of experiments. When these activities are disconnected, understanding the relationship between source code, circuit transformations, simulation results, and experimental evidence becomes more difficult. QORE aims to provide a unified engineering environment in which these relationships remain visible. The central problem QORE addresses: How can quantum developers move from quantum source code to an inspectable, tested, measurable, and reproducible experiment without losing the context connecting each stage? QORE complements existing quantum frameworks rather than assuming that established tools lack these capabilities. Its differentiation must be demonstrated through integration, transparency, reproducibility, and measurable engineering contributions. 3. Core Product Principles 3.1 AI proposes AI assistance can explain code, suggest circuit transformations, identify possible issues, and recommend experiments. Suggestions must be distinguishable from verified outcomes. 3.2 Verification checks Supported circuits and transformations should be checked using appropriate validation methods. Syntax validity alone must never be represented as proof of semantic equivalence. 3.3 Experiments provide the evidence Simulation results, circuit metrics, optimization comparisons, configurations, and validation outcomes must come from real operations. Every saved experiment should retain enough information to understand how its results were produced. 3.4 Human approval controls changes AI-generated or automatically generated candidate transformations must not silently overwrite the original program. Users should inspect and approve changes. 3.5 Scientific honesty is mandatory QORE must distinguish theoretical values, simulated measurements, estimates, and actual hardware measurements. It must not claim quantum advantage, superior performance, or guaranteed optimization without supporting evidence. 4. Phase 1 MVP Scope Build a responsive, desktop-oriented web application with six connected functional areas: 1. QORE Studio — quantum code editing and project management. 2. QORE Circuit Viewer — circuit visualization and resource analysis. 3. QORE Lab — real local simulation and measurement feedback. 4. QORE Forge — optimization, candidate comparison, and validation. 5. QORE Intelligence — optional context-aware AI assistance. 6. QORE Research — experiment history, reproducibility, and provenance. All six areas must use consistent project and circuit data. If AI integration cannot be completed reliably, the other five areas must continue working. 4.1 QORE Studio Create the primary quantum development workspace. Required features: - Editable source-code editor. - Syntax highlighting for the supported programming format. - New, open, rename, and save project operations. - Working example projects. - Parse, validate, and run actions. - Clear error messages for invalid or unsupported code. - Execution status and loading indicators. - Unsaved-change awareness. - Project navigation and experiment history. Use Monaco Editor if compatible with the existing stack. For Phase 1, implement a documented and tested subset of Qiskit-based quantum programs. Do not claim arbitrary Python or full Qiskit compatibility unless actually implemented and tested. 4.2 QORE-IR — Quantum Intermediate Representation QORE-IR is the shared representation connecting the development workflow. It must provide a consistent source of truth for: - Qubit declarations. - Supported quantum operations. - Gate parameters. - Control and target relationships. - Measurements. - Classical output mappings. - Circuit ordering. - Circuit serialization. - Resource metrics. - Simulation preparation. - Optimization transformations. - Validation. - Experiment persistence. Define a versioned schema and document supported operations. The parser must convert supported source programs into a real framework circuit object or a validated normalized representation. Do not use fragile text matching as a substitute for parsing executable language constructs. The frontend visualizer, analysis engine, simulator, and optimizer must not independently invent different interpretations of the same circuit. Where framework-native circuit objects are used, define how they map into QORE-IR and back. 4.3 QORE Circuit Viewer Render the actual circuit derived from QORE-IR. Display: - Qubit wires and labels. - Quantum gates and their parameters. - Controlled gates and connections. - Measurement operations. - Classical output connections. - Circuit depth. - Gate count. - Two-qubit gate count. - Applicable gate-type statistics. Circuit visualization must update when a new supported program is parsed. Provide clear feedback for unsupported gates and structures. Use SVG rendering or an appropriate circuit visualization library. Avoid static diagrams presented as live circuit visualizations. 4.4 QORE Lab Integrate a real local quantum simulator using Qiskit and Qiskit Aer, or a compatible documented alternative. Required features: - Execute supported circuits. - Configure shot count. - Display actual measurement counts. - Calculate and display measurement probabilities. - Display circuit and simulator metadata. - Show execution errors and warnings. - Distinguish theoretical probabilities from finite-shot measurements. - Preserve the configuration used for an experiment. Required demonstration: Bell-state circuit Implement a working Bell-state example: 1. Apply a Hadamard gate to the first qubit. 2. Apply a CNOT gate using the first qubit as control and the second as target. 3. Measure both qubits. Under ideal conditions, the expected outcomes are 00 and 11, each with probability approximately 50%. The other two outcomes should have probability approximately zero. Actual finite-shot measurements may vary. Account for Qiskit's classical bit-string ordering and explain the displayed mapping clearly. Use this experiment to demonstrate circuit construction, visualization, execution, measurement distributions, and interpretation. Do not present Bell-state correlation as evidence of quantum computational advantage. 4.5 QORE Forge — Optimization and Verification QORE Forge is the principal technical component of Phase 1. Implement a working pipeline that creates an optimized candidate from an original circuit using a supported quantum compiler optimization pass. Required functionality: - Preserve the original circuit. - Generate a separate candidate. - Record the optimization pass and settings. - Render both circuit versions. - Calculate comparable metrics. - Display absolute and relative differences where meaningful. - Explain the transformation at a useful level. - Validate supported semantic properties. - Allow the user to inspect and approve the candidate. Metrics should include applicable measures such as: - Gate count. - Circuit depth. - Two-qubit gate count. - Qubit count. - Gate-type distribution. Document whether measurements, barriers, and other instructions contribute to each metric. Use established compiler optimizations as the baseline. Clearly identify framework-provided transformations versus any original QORE-specific method. Do not hardcode performance improvements. If optimization does not improve a metric, display the actual result. Validation requirements Use a suitable method for the supported circuit and transformation, such as statevector comparison up to global phase for applicable small unitary circuits, or output-distribution comparison under controlled equivalent simulation settings. Handle measurements, classical operations, and unsupported constructs according to the selected validation method. Report one of the following as appropriate: - Validated under the stated method. - Validation failed. - Validation unavailable. - Validation inconclusive. Do not equate successful parsing or compilation with proof of equivalence. 4.6 QORE Intelligence Provide an optional AI assistant grounded in the current project and available execution data. It should be able to: - Explain supported quantum source code. - Describe gates and circuit structure. - Interpret simulator outputs. - Explain resource metrics. - Summarize optimization differences. - Suggest possible improvements. - Help diagnose errors. - Recommend experiments. AI responses must be grounded in actual code, circuit metadata, and results when relevant. The assistant must never claim that it executed a program or verified a transformation when that operation did not occur. Use a server-side API integration, such as Gemini, only when credentials and access are available. Keep credentials server-side, use environment variables or an appropriate secret manager, and provide graceful handling when the AI service is unavailable. AI must remain an optional assistance layer rather than a dependency for core quantum functionality. 4.7 QORE Research — Reproducibility Ledger Create persistent project and experiment records. Store applicable information such as: - Project and experiment identifiers. - Source code. - Source-code SHA-256 hash. - QORE-IR version. - Framework and simulator versions. - Backend identifier. - Shot count. - Random seed, where supported and configured. - Circuit metrics. - Optimization settings. - Original and optimized representations. - Simulation results. - Validation method and outcome. - Execution metadata. - Timestamps. - Errors and warnings. Use SQLite for the initial persistence layer. Provide the ability to list, save, reopen, and inspect previous experiments. Historical results must remain distinguishable from newly executed results. A source hash supports identification of code content, but must not be presented as proof of execution correctness. Preserve the associated configuration and relevant dependency metadata as well. If exact reproducibility cannot be guaranteed, clearly state why. 5. Complete End-to-End Workflow The flagship demonstration must work through one connected interface: Open Project → Edit Code → Parse → Visualize → Analyze → Simulate → Optimize → Validate → Compare → Save → Reopen 1. Open the Bell-state example. 2. Parse the supported program into QORE-IR. 3. Render the actual circuit. 4. Display circuit resource metrics. 5. Execute a genuine local simulation. 6. Show measurement counts and probabilities. 7. Create an optimized candidate using a real compiler pass. 8. Compare original and candidate circuits. 9. Run an appropriate validation check. 10. Save the source, configuration, results, and provenance. 11. Reopen the experiment and confirm that its historical record is preserved. Every stage must operate on actual application data. A visually complete screen without working backend functionality does not satisfy this requirement. 6. Architecture and Technology Stack Follow the architecture specified in the submitted QORE presentation. Frontend - React. - TypeScript. - Tailwind CSS. - Monaco Editor. - SVG-based circuit rendering or a suitable visualization library. - Charts for measurement distributions and metric comparisons. Backend - Python. - FastAPI. - Pydantic. - Qiskit. - Qiskit Aer or a compatible local simulator. - SQLite. - pytest. Architecture layers Presentation layer: IDE, editor, circuit viewer, simulation panels, optimization comparisons, experiment history. Application layer: project workflows, execution orchestration, validation, optimization, experiment management. Quantum processing layer: parsing, QORE-IR conversion, circuit construction, simulation, resource analysis, optimization and validation. Persistence layer: projects, experiment records, configurations, results, provenance and version metadata. Use structured API contracts and consistent error responses. The application must start locally with documented setup instructions. Adapt to the existing repository rather than replacing a working architecture without justification. 7. Safe Execution Architecture The submitted presentation specifies static AST pre-validation, a controlled namespace, an isolated runtime, and deterministic resource caps. Implement a security-conscious approach that reflects these goals. Required safeguards: - Restrict the supported input constructs. - Validate source before execution. - Avoid unrestricted execution of arbitrary user-provided Python. - Use a controlled namespace. - Apply execution timeouts and resource limits. - Isolate execution where feasible. - Limit filesystem and network access. - Validate API inputs. - Keep API credentials out of the frontend. - Handle oversized and malformed requests. - Prevent a failed run from crashing the entire application. Static AST validation alone is not a complete sandbox. If execution isolation cannot be implemented reliably, construct supported circuits through a constrained interpreter or controlled circuit-building layer instead of executing arbitrary Python. Document the actual security guarantees and limitations. 8. Extension API and Future Ecosystem Design QORE's internal architecture to support future extension points. Potential extension categories include: Hardware connectors: provider-specific quantum processing unit adapters. Compiler passes: additional circuit transformations. AI and analytics plugins: diagnostic tools and experiment analysis. A future extension contract may expose interfaces conceptually similar to: - provider.execute(job) - pass.run(circuit) - plugin.analyze(run) These are interface concepts, not a claim that a stable public plugin API already exists. For Phase 1, implement only the extension points that are necessary and testable. Document future interfaces instead of creating empty integrations. 9. Reproducibility and Experiment Telemetry Every experiment should have a traceable record connecting its source, configuration, execution, and output. The submitted presentation identifies source hashing, side-by-side comparisons, total variation distance (TVD), and persistent audit trails as important elements. Implement these carefully: - Calculate source hashes from actual source content. - Preserve the backend and simulator configuration. - Record shot count and seed when applicable. - Save original and optimized circuit metrics. - Preserve the results used in a comparison. - Store the validation method and outcome. - Calculate TVD only when valid probability distributions are available. For discrete probability distributions \(P\) and \(Q\), total variation distance is: \ \operatorname{TVD}(P,Q)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_x |P(x)-Q(x)| \ Explain what two distributions are being compared. For example, a simulated measurement distribution may be compared with an ideal reference distribution. Do not copy illustrative telemetry values from a mockup and present them as measured application results. 10. Interface and Visual Design System The implementation must follow the submitted QORE presentation's visual identity. Color palette - Primary background: 080B14 - Panel background: 0F1523 or a visually compatible deep navy. - Primary text: F4F7FF - Secondary text: accessible muted gray. - Cyan accent: 57D9FF - Violet accent: 9A83FF - Borders: subtle blue-gray with restrained cyan or violet emphasis. Use the values above as design tokens, allowing adjustments only when necessary for contrast and consistency with the presentation. Visual language - Dark scientific developer-tool aesthetic. - Bold white headings. - Cyan monospace section labels and technical metadata. - Violet accents for secondary technical emphasis. - Thin borders. - Subtle radial ambient glows. - Carefully layered navy surfaces. - Restrained transitions and hover states. - Clear visual hierarchy. - Consistent spacing and alignment. Avoid generic dashboard styling, excessive gradients, decorative glass effects, unnecessary animation, and inconsistent colors. Application layout Left sidebar: projects, source files, examples, experiments. Main workspace: source editor and circuit visualization. Results panel: simulation output, measurements, resource metrics, optimization and validation status. Optional assistant panel: context-aware AI assistance. Top navigation: project controls and the main workflow actions. Make the layout responsive. Desktop is the primary target, while smaller screens should retain access to essential functions through appropriate panels or tabs. Interface states Implement real states for: - Empty workspace. - Project loaded. - Parsing. - Parse success or failure. - Simulation in progress. - Simulation results. - Simulator error. - Optimization in progress. - Optimization results. - No measurable improvement. - Validation success, failure or unavailable. - Experiment saved. - Experiment reopened. - AI unavailable. Every primary button must perform its advertised action. 11. Competitive Positioning QORE should be positioned as an integrated, evidence-driven quantum development environment that can complement existing quantum software ecosystems. Relevant ecosystems include Qiskit, Cirq, Microsoft Quantum Development Kit, and OpenQASM-compatible tools. Do not claim that QORE replaces these tools or provides superior quantum computation simply because it combines their general workflow stages. The defensible value proposition is the connection between: - Source code and circuit representation. - Circuit visualization and resource metrics. - Simulation and measurement analysis. - Optimization and candidate validation. - Experiment outputs and reproducible provenance. Any claim of novelty or performance improvement must be supported by actual implementation evidence or reproducible measurements. 12. Testing and Acceptance Criteria Parsing tests Test valid supported programs, invalid syntax, unsupported operations, malformed inputs, and measurement mapping. Circuit tests Verify gate order, control-target relationships, visualization consistency, and metric calculations. Simulation tests Test Bell-state behavior, shot count, probability calculations, bit ordering, and execution failures. Optimization tests Confirm that the original circuit is preserved, the candidate comes from a real optimization pass, metrics are calculated consistently, and non-improving results are reported honestly. Validation tests Verify the selected equivalence or behavioral comparison method and confirm that unsupported cases are not incorrectly marked as validated. Persistence tests Test project saving, experiment creation, retrieval, reopening, and preservation of historical results. Security tests Test request validation, supported-source restrictions, secret handling, resource limits, and error recovery. Final acceptance test A user must be able to complete the entire Bell-state workflow in the actual running application. The application must execute real operations, display their actual outputs, and reopen the saved experiment. Report only tests that were actually executed. 13. Implementation Roadmap Phase 1A — Foundation Inspect the existing codebase, preserve working functionality, establish the supported source subset, define QORE-IR, and implement backend/frontend communication. Phase 1B — Core Quantum Workflow Implement Studio, parsing, circuit visualization, circuit metrics, local simulation, and the Bell-state demonstration. Phase 1C — QORE Forge Implement optimization, original-versus-candidate comparison, appropriate validation, and transparent reporting. Phase 1D — QORE Research Implement SQLite persistence, experiment provenance, saved project retrieval, and experiment reopening. Phase 1E — Product Quality Apply the final visual system, improve accessibility and responsive layouts, add loading and failure states, and execute the automated tests. Phase 1F — Optional Intelligence Integrate grounded AI assistance only after the core workflow is reliable. Do not start future platform modules while critical Phase 1 acceptance criteria remain unmet. 14. Long-Term Roadmap The presentation identifies three horizons. Horizon 1 — Foundation - Local quantum IDE. - QORE-IR. - Circuit visualization. - Aer simulation. - Forge optimization. - Debugging and experiment persistence. Horizon 2 — Connected Development - Cloud synchronization. - Multi-user collaboration. - Hardware and provider adapters. - Hybrid quantum-classical workflows. - Expanded optimization and debugging. Horizon 3 — Broader Quantum Infrastructure - Expanded framework integrations. - Advanced AI-assisted engineering. - Research and benchmarking infrastructure. - Support for larger and more sophisticated quantum workloads. - Enterprise-oriented and industrial workflows where technically justified. These horizons represent the product direction, not completed Phase 1 features. 15. Definition of Done Phase 1 is complete when: - The application starts using documented instructions. - Users can edit and save supported quantum programs. - QORE-IR consistently represents the supported circuits. - The circuit viewer reflects actual parsed data. - The local simulator returns genuine results. - Resource metrics are computed from real circuit objects. - QORE Forge creates and compares real optimization candidates. - Appropriate validation is performed and accurately reported. - Experiments can be saved and reopened. - The provenance record captures relevant source and execution metadata. - The visual design matches QORE's submitted identity. - Critical automated tests have been executed. - Unsupported operations and incomplete capabilities are documented. - No fake metrics, hardcoded execution results, or simulated success states are presented as real. 16. Required Final Engineering Report At the end of implementation, provide: 1. Repository assessment and existing functionality. 2. Features implemented. 3. Actual technology stack. 4. Architecture and QORE-IR design. 5. Supported source constructs and limitations. 6. Setup and execution instructions. 7. Actual automated test results. 8. Actual Bell-state simulation output. 9. Actual optimization comparison. 10. Validation method and result. 11. Persistence and experiment-reopening results. 12. Security measures and remaining limitations. 13. Known bugs and unfinished features. 14. Screenshots of the running application. 15. Recommended next engineering priorities. Clearly distinguish implemented features, verified outcomes, planned features, and untested claims. Do not fabricate successful tests, performance gains, circuit equivalence, or execution statistics. Final Implementation Directive Inspect the existing repository first. Preserve working code and existing functionality wherever possible. Implement QORE as a cohesive quantum software development environment following the submitted presentation's visual identity, modular architecture, and evidence-driven philosophy. Prioritize the complete workflow: Write Code → Visualize → Simulate → Analyze → Optimize → Validate → Compare → Save → Reopen Use genuine quantum framework operations, real simulation results, transparent optimization comparisons, appropriate verification, and persistent experiment provenance. Build the smallest complete and reliable implementation that satisfies the acceptance criteria. Run the available tests, fix failures, document limitations, and report the actual results. The goal is not to make QORE look finished. The goal is to make its core engineering workflow genuinely work.

title: Production operations
text: Production operations QORE serves the React workbench and FastAPI API from one origin. This release intentionally has no account, login, OAuth, or email-confirmation flow. Editable Explorer source is retained in browser storage. Backend projects, runs, workspace records, and Ledger evidence use SQLite and an opaque browser-specific HttpOnly cookie. Simulation remains a bounded Qiskit environment rather than arbitrary Python, a general shell, or a hardware-job service. Runtime architecture The browser loads a static Vite build and calls same-origin /api routes. AnonymousWorkspace validates or creates a random UUID cookie, then scopes every database operation to guest:uuid. The cookie is HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax; production adds Secure. It is a capability for one browser profile, not proof of a person's identity. Anyone with control of that browser profile can use its QORE workspace. FastAPI validates request shape, size, origin, and host. Circuit work is passed to a bounded worker with explicit qubit, operation, shot, and timeout limits. SQLite stores project and evidence records. Gemini calls are optional, rate-limited, and server-side; the key is never accepted in JSON or compiled into the frontend. Required host settings | Variable | Production value | | --- | --- | | QORE_ENV | production | | QORE_STORAGE | sqlite | | QORE_DB_PATH | A path on the mounted persistent disk | | QORE_PUBLIC_URL | The public HTTPS origin | | GEMINI_API_KEY | Optional secret entered in the host dashboard | | GEMINI_MODEL | An allowed Gemini model identifier | Never put a Gemini or database credential in a VITE_ variable, Dockerfile, committed environment file, source comment, issue, screenshot, or CI log. The checked-in .env.example contains names and safe defaults only. Render and Docker Build from the repository root with Dockerfile. The image installs the Python runtime, copies the built frontend, installs QORE, and starts Uvicorn on the platform-provided PORT. Attach a persistent disk and point QORE_DB_PATH into that mount. Without a disk, browser files still survive refreshes, but backend projects, runs, and Ledger records can disappear whenever Render replaces the container. After deployment, inspect /api/health. It should report status: ok, storage: sqlite, auth_configured: false, and auth_required: false. ai_available confirms that the server process can see configuration; a real QI request verifies provider connectivity. Never expose the value while debugging. Release verification From the repository root run: powershell & .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest backend/tests -q & .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts/production_acceptance.py & .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts/security_checker.py --check & .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts/frontend_auditor.py Set-Location frontend pnpm build pnpm test:ui Tests distinguish mocked browser/provider checks from real numerical simulation. Validate Explorer by creating nested folders, renaming a subtree, editing two files, refreshing, deleting a folder, undoing it, and restoring another item from Trash. Validate QI in every view, including one question without a circuit and one source-matched simulation explanation. GitHub Actions and promotion The quality workflow installs pinned package-manager and language versions, runs the daily quality report, builds the frontend, starts the local production server, and runs Playwright contracts. Do not promote an editing commit while a required job is red. A secret scan failure is a release failure even if the application builds. The recommended flow is editing branch → local verification → pull request checks → production branch/main. Generated evidence, databases, browser profiles, dependencies, and promotional recordings remain ignored. Only intentional source, documentation, lockfiles, migrations, and reproducible public assets belong in a release commit. QI Assistant operations QI uses GEMINI_API_KEY and GEMINI_MODEL from the backend process. The API assembles the active view, file name, bounded workspace summary, diagnostics, optional source, and source-matched run evidence. A model answer cannot trigger arbitrary commands. The local QI command map supports a small explicit set of QORE actions, while simulation and optimization still pass through normal validated endpoints. Rate limits are process-local: ten assistant calls per browser workspace per minute, two simultaneous provider calls, a bounded admission wait, and a provider timeout. Configure provider-side budgets and monitoring separately. Multiple replicas need a shared rate limiter and job queue before horizontal scaling. Backups and recovery Back up the mounted SQLite database using a consistent snapshot method. Test restore into a separate service before treating backups as reliable. Browser source is separate: users should export important files before clearing site data or changing browser profiles. Trash provides a 48-hour application recovery window; it is not a replacement for database backups. Security boundary Origin checks, trusted hosts, request limits, constrained circuit parsing, isolated browser scopes, and secure headers reduce risk. They do not turn an account-free public deployment into authenticated multi-tenant storage. Use this release for local, personal, demonstration, or controlled-access environments. Add a reviewed identity layer before hosting confidential work for unrelated users. The previously committed privileged database credential must be rotated in its provider dashboard. Removing it from the current Dockerfile prevents new exposure but does not invalidate copies already present in Git history.

title: Bloch spheres and reduced states
text: Bloch spheres and reduced states The Bloch sphere represents a single-qubit density matrix with coordinates x, y, and z. Pure states lie on the surface; mixed states lie inside. QORE reports purity and labels whether the reduced state is pure within its numerical policy. For an entangled register, an individual qubit can have a centered Bloch vector even though the complete multi-qubit state is pure. This is expected for GHZ and Bell states: local information is mixed while correlations live in the joint state. A centered vector is therefore not by itself evidence of failed preparation. Rotate the 3D view for orientation, but read the numeric vector, purity, source, and run metadata for analysis. Animation is a navigation aid rather than experimental evidence.

title: Circuit equivalence
text: Circuit equivalence Forge compares original and candidate operators up to global phase for circuits within the six-qubit validation bound. It also checks terminal measurement mapping. A small numerical residual within the documented tolerance supports equivalence for that exact method and source; it is not a universal proof for larger or dynamic circuits. Gate-count or depth improvement does not imply equivalence. Conversely, an equivalent candidate may use more gates after basis decomposition. Review validation status, method, residual, measurement mapping, warnings, and source before applying a candidate. After application, rerun the changed source to produce fresh sampled evidence.

title: Quantum computing foundations
text: Quantum computing foundations A qubit is described by complex amplitudes whose squared magnitudes sum to one. Relative phase affects later interference even when it is invisible in an immediate computational-basis measurement. Multiple qubits live in a joint state space; entanglement means that state cannot be separated into independent single-qubit states. Gates are unitary transformations. Measurement converts a quantum state into classical outcomes sampled according to probability, so finite-shot counts fluctuate. A simulator can retain exact statevector evidence before measurement and also sample shots; those are different objects and should not be conflated. QORE makes this distinction visible through circuit structure, ideal probabilities, sampled distributions, amplitudes, reduced Bloch vectors, and metadata. It does not claim hardware execution or quantum advantage. Use small circuits to form a prediction first, then compare the recorded result and limitation statement.

title: Measurement and bit ordering
text: Measurement and bit ordering Measurement maps qubits into classical bits. The displayed bitstring places the highest classical index on the left and c0 on the right, following the recorded Qiskit convention. A mapping such as q0 → c1 means the observed value of qubit zero appears in the second classical position, not necessarily at the right edge. Counts are integers summing to shots. Sampled probabilities are counts divided by shots. Ideal probabilities come from the noiseless unitary prefix under the same mapping. Total variation distance summarizes the difference between distributions but does not explain its cause; sampling, modeled noise, mapping errors, or changed source must be considered separately. Always read the bit-ordering metadata attached to the run. Do not relabel strings to match intuition, because that destroys reproducibility.

title: QAOA and graph-cut experiments
text: QAOA and graph-cut experiments QAOA alternates a cost evolution encoding an optimization objective with a mixer that redistributes amplitude. For a graph-cut example, computational-basis strings represent partitions and the cost rewards edges crossing the partition. Parameters determine the interference pattern; measurement samples candidate strings rather than proving an optimum. Use openqasm/qaoa_cut.qasm as a four-qubit inspection case. Verify its gate structure, matrix within display limits, ideal amplitudes, sampled distribution, and classical mapping. Record shots, seed, simulator method, and source hash. A high-frequency bitstring is evidence from that configured run—not a guarantee about every parameter choice or hardware execution.

title: Reproducibility and evidence
text: Reproducibility and evidence Reproducibility requires exact source, source hash, shot count, seed, simulator method, noise settings, dependency versions, bit mapping, and validation scope. QORE stores these fields with runs and Ledger snapshots so a later reader can distinguish source identity from execution environment. A fixed simulator seed makes sampling repeatable within the recorded software environment, but native libraries and framework versions can change details. A source hash proves content identity, not physical correctness. Hardware reproducibility would additionally require backend calibration, queue, layout, compilation, and mitigation records, which this release does not claim. Name experiments by question and configuration, preserve failed runs as failures, and never replace missing evidence with assistant prose.

title: QORE-IR and Supported Quantum Subset
text: QORE-IR and Supported Quantum Subset 1. Supported Quantum Subset QORE Phase 1 implements a strictly controlled subset of Qiskit Python programs. Arbitrary Python code is parsed via Python's ast module and walked through a restricted visitor allowlist. No user code is ever passed to eval, exec, or dynamic module loaders. 1.1 Supported Imports - from qiskit import QuantumCircuit - import qiskit - import math / from math import pi, tau, e - import numpy / from numpy import pi, e 1.2 Circuit Declarations Programs must declare exactly one QuantumCircuit instance: python from qiskit import QuantumCircuit qc = QuantumCircuit(qubits, classical_bits) - Maximum qubits: 10 (MAX_QUBITS = 10) - Maximum classical bits: 10 (MAX_CLBITS = 10) - Maximum operations: 500 (MAX_OPERATIONS = 500) - Maximum source size: 32 KB (MAX_SOURCE_BYTES = 32768) 1.3 Supported Gates and Operations Unitary gates supported in Phase 1: - 1-qubit parameter-free: id (i), x, y, z, h, s, sdg, t, tdg, sx, sxdg - 1-qubit parameterized: rx(theta, q), ry(theta, q), rz(theta, q), p(theta, q) - 1-qubit 3-parameter unitary: u(theta, phi, lam, q) - 2-qubit parameter-free: cx (cnot), cy, cz, ch, swap, ecr - 2-qubit parameterized: cp(theta, c, t), crx, cry, crz, rxx, ryy, rzz, rzx - 3-qubit gates: ccx (toffoli), cswap - Barriers: qc.barrier() or qc.barrier(0, 1) - Measurements: qc.measure(qubit, clbit) (strictly terminal; mid-circuit measurements and conditional reset are rejected) - Global phase assignment: qc.global_phase = float_val --- 2. QORE-IR Specification (Version 1.0) QORE-IR connects Studio (editor), Circuit Viewer (SVG visualizer), Lab (Aer simulator), Forge (transpiler/optimizer), and Research (provenance ledger) into an unambiguous shared intermediate representation. 2.1 Schema Definition json { "version": "1.0", "num_qubits": 2, "num_clbits": 2, "global_phase": 0.0, "operations": { "name": "h", "qubits": 0, "clbits": , "params": }, { "name": "cx", "qubits": 0, 1, "clbits": , "params": }, { "name": "measure", "qubits": 0, "clbits": 0, "params": }, { "name": "measure", "qubits": 1, "clbits": 1, "params": } } 2.2 Metrics Schema Circuit resource metrics are computed directly from the canonical circuit representation: - gate_count: Total unitary operations (measurements and barriers are strictly excluded). - depth: Circuit depth computed via Qiskit's DAG (includes measurements, excludes barriers). - two_qubit_gate_count: Unitary operations acting on exactly two qubits. - qubits / clbits: Register counts. - measurement_count / barrier_count: Tracked separately for full accountability. - gate_types: Breakdown dictionary of unitary gates by type (e.g. {"h": 1, "cx": 1}). --- 3. Equivalence and Verification Model QORE Forge optimizes circuits using standard Qiskit transpilation passes (optimization_level = 0..3). Verification evaluates semantic equivalence: 1. Operator Equivalence (Unitary Portion): For circuits with $\le 6$ qubits without mid-circuit measurements, QORE computes the full unitary operators $U_{\text{orig}}$ and $U_{\text{cand}}$ using qiskit.quantum_info.Operator. The Hilbert-Schmidt inner product normalized process fidelity is computed: $$F_{\text{process}} = \frac{|\operatorname{Tr}(U_{\text{orig}}^\dagger U_{\text{cand}})|^2}{d^2}$$ where $d = 2^n$. The candidate is verified if $1 - F \le 10^{-9}$ and the global phase difference $\Delta\theta$ is bounded. 2. Measurement Destination Invariance: Every terminal measurement mapping $(q_i \to c_j)$ in the original circuit must match the candidate circuit identically. Reordered or missing measurement assignments cause validation to fail.

title: QORE documentation

Use evidence within its scope Ideal amplitudes describe a noiseless state before measurement. Shot counts are finite samples from the selected simulator and noise settings. title: HTTP API reference
text: HTTP API reference All application routes are under /api and return JSON. Errors use {"error":{"code":"…","message":"…","details":…}}. Unknown fields are rejected. Source is limited to 32 KiB and request bodies to 96 KiB. Service and source GET /health reports runtime versions, AI availability, storage mode, limits, and the disabled-auth state. POST /parse accepts {source} and returns QORE-IR, metrics, warnings, source hash, and bounded visual evidence. POST /simulate adds shots, seed, optional noise and method. POST /optimize adds compilation level and seed. Projects and evidence GET /projects, POST /projects, GET /projects/{id}, and PUT /projects/{id} manage named source records within the current browser workspace. GET /runs and GET /runs/{id} expose recorded executions. POST /experiments creates an immutable Ledger snapshot from exact source and optional source-matched run IDs. GET /experiments lists summaries; GET /experiments/{id} returns complete evidence. QI Assistant POST /assistant accepts question, optional source, view, file_name, workspace_summary, diagnostics, and optional simulation or optimization IDs. Referenced runs must belong to the same browser scope, have the expected kind, be successful, and match the submitted source hash. A response is {available,answer,model?}. Unavailability is reported honestly and never replaced with fabricated numerical output. Workspace GET /workspace returns active files, folders, Trash, active ID, server time, and retention. PUT file/folder routes require UUID identifiers and expected versions. DELETE soft-deletes; POST restore and undo recover eligible entries; PATCH state selects an active file. Paths are normalized relative names, never host filesystem paths. Security semantics There are no auth routes. The qore_workspace cookie is assigned by the server and must be sent same-origin. Cross-origin writes are rejected. UUIDs are identifiers, not authorization; every lookup also applies the browser workspace scope.

title: Architecture and trust boundaries
text: Architecture and trust boundaries QORE is a single-origin React and FastAPI application. React owns the interactive workbench; FastAPI validates API contracts and coordinates bounded quantum workers; Qiskit and Aer provide circuit semantics; SQLite stores projects and immutable evidence. Browser storage holds editable Explorer source so typing and refresh recovery do not depend on network latency. Request path Every API request crosses trusted-host, origin, body-size, and schema checks before application logic. A random HttpOnly workspace cookie selects a SQLite namespace. The client never supplies an owner ID. Parse, simulate, and optimize requests enter a process-local budget and a two-slot worker gate. CPU-heavy quantum work runs outside the async event loop and is subject to a 30-second timeout. Data classes Editable workspace files are mutable working material. Projects are named source records. Runs are append-oriented simulation or optimization results. Ledger experiments are immutable snapshots linking exact source hashes to compatible runs. Editing a file clears live UI evidence but never rewrites a saved run or experiment. AI boundary QI Assistant receives a bounded context assembled by the backend. Gemini credentials remain in the server environment. Source and questions are treated as untrusted content, not system instructions. Local QI commands map to a small allowlist of existing UI actions; model text cannot execute arbitrary operations. Deployment boundary The container is replaceable; durable state must live on a mounted disk addressed by QORE_DB_PATH. Browser state belongs to one origin and profile. The anonymous cookie isolates browser workspaces but is not verified identity, so this release is appropriate for personal, local, demonstration, or controlled-access use—not confidential public multi-tenancy. Failure behavior Validation failures return structured errors without stack traces. Provider failure does not disable Studio, Lab, Forge, or Ledger. A worker timeout records an unsuccessful run when possible. Missing durable storage can lose backend evidence while leaving browser source intact, which is why UI save state and operations monitoring must distinguish those layers.

title: Supported circuit language
text: Supported circuit language QORE accepts OpenQASM 2 and a deliberately constrained Qiskit-style Python subset. It parses structure instead of executing arbitrary Python. Supported programs construct QuantumCircuit, apply documented gates, add barriers, and perform terminal measurement. Circuit aliases, register sizes, indices, numeric parameters, and bounded loops must be statically understandable. Imports outside the allowlist, file access, networking, subprocesses, reflection, dynamic evaluation, arbitrary function calls, and operating-system APIs are rejected. Installing an SDK does not expand the public editor language. This boundary keeps the circuit surface reviewable and makes resource limits enforceable. QORE supports up to 10 qubits, 10 classical bits, 500 operations, and 32 KiB of UTF-8 source. Measurement must be terminal for the current ideal-state and equivalence workflows. Dynamic classical control and mid-circuit measurement are outside the Phase 1 contract. OpenQASM bitstrings follow the recorded classical mapping. Never infer qubit order from visual position alone; read the result's bit-ordering field. For portable experiments, specify shots, seed, method, noise parameters, and source exactly, then preserve the run in Ledger.

title: Runtime limits and compatibility
text: Runtime limits and compatibility | Limit | Value | | --- | ---: | | Source | 32 KiB UTF-8 | | Request body | 96 KiB | | Qubits / classical bits | 10 / 10 | | Operations | 500 | | Shots | 1–100,000 | | Worker timeout | 30 seconds | | Concurrent quantum jobs | 2 per process | | Operator equivalence | Up to 6 qubits | | Matrix display | Up to 4 qubits | | Ideal amplitudes and Bloch data | Up to 6 qubits | Limits protect responsiveness; they do not predict performance exactly. Simulation cost depends on method, circuit structure, entanglement, noise, and native-library behavior. A circuit below every numeric cap can still time out. Multiple replicas need shared admission control to enforce global budgets. QORE supports bounded Aer simulation and transpiler analysis. It does not promise arbitrary Qiskit compatibility, external service authentication, cloud hardware submission, pulse scheduling, unrestricted Python, or a real shell. Unsupported capability must return an explicit error rather than silently changing semantics.

title: Workspace API and recovery model
text: Workspace API and recovery model Workspace entries have a stable UUID, relative path, type, optional source kind, version, timestamps, and deletion metadata. File source may be empty. Folder operations cover the active subtree atomically. Expected versions prevent stale tabs from silently overwriting newer server state. Deleting creates a Trash batch and sets an exact expiry 48 hours later. Undo restores the latest eligible batch. Direct restore checks every destination first; a conflict aborts the whole operation. Expired content is unavailable even before physical cleanup. Tombstones prevent stale clients from recreating a deleted identity. Paths use slash-separated safe segments. Empty, dot, parent, backslash, control, and reserved characters are rejected. A workspace path is a logical QORE name and never grants host filesystem access. The server allows 1,000 active-plus-Trash entries and 16 MiB of aggregate retained source per browser workspace. These server constraints are distinct from browser storage quotas. Export important source before clearing site data or migrating origins.

title: Local execution guarantees and limitations
text: Local execution guarantees and limitations QORE is designed for a single user on loopback. Start with --host 127.0.0.1. It has no multi-user authentication, tenancy, or internet-facing deployment security. Source handling User source is parsed using Python's AST and interpreted through a closed circuit-building grammar. It is never passed to exec, eval, a shell, dynamic import, or a Python runtime namespace. Supported imports are declarations recognized by the interpreter, not general Python imports. Filesystem/network calls, attributes outside the defined grammar, arbitrary functions/classes, comprehensions, while loops, exceptions and unsupported constructs are rejected. The engine documents exact permitted constructs in QUANTUM.md. The AST interpreter and framework mapping enforce source bytes, AST/numeric/iteration limits, qubit/classical-bit/operation caps, finite numeric values, supported gate arity, bit indices, and terminal-only measurements. Exact full-operator verification is capped separately at six qubits. No assertion of equivalence is made when that method is unavailable. Runtime controls Each parse/simulate/optimize job uses a fresh subprocess through a fixed qore.worker entry point and structured JSON stdin. The parent imposes a 30-second wall-clock timeout and kills/waits for the worker on timeout. There are at most two active quantum jobs, with a two-second queue wait followed by HTTP 429. Numerical libraries and Aer use limited CPU parallelism. API inputs cap 10 qubits, 10 classical bits, 500 operations, 100000 shots and 32 KiB UTF-8 source. JSON bodies are capped at 96 KiB regardless of their advertised content length. The worker receives a small environment allowlist; AI keys are excluded. User source has no operation that can read files, access the network or spawn processes. This is not an operating-system sandbox: trusted Python/Qiskit/native dependencies retain their normal OS privileges, and no hard OS memory quota or network namespace is configured on Windows. Resource bounds reduce expected resource use; they do not protect against an exploitable defect in a dependency. Untrusted multi-tenant hosting would need containers/VMs, OS quotas, network restrictions, authentication and rate limits. API, secrets and persistence Pydantic rejects unexpected fields, malformed types, out-of-range values and oversized inputs. Requests use a consistent error envelope; internal exception details and provider errors are not returned to clients. Trusted host checks and explicit loopback Origin checks reject cross-origin writes. Cross-site browser requests are rejected. Same-origin production serving and Vite proxying avoid broad CORS permissions. These controls are not authentication against malicious local processes. SQL uses parameter binding. Runs and experiments are append-only through the API, and experiment creation retrieves trusted run records by ID and checks exact source hashes and run types. The client cannot submit invented counts as evidence. Local users with filesystem access can modify SQLite; there is no cryptographic execution attestation or tamper-proof audit trail. Failed runs are retained with source, configuration, timestamp and error. Gemini credentials exist only in server environment variables and never frontend bundles. The assistant only sends context after the user asks a question. Source and results are treated as untrusted text in the AI system prompt. AI output is advisory text, never executable code or automatic source changes. No logs intentionally include API keys. Deployment boundary Do not expose this Phase 1 server to a public network. Security verification results in ENGINEERING_REPORT.md describe tests actually executed, not a formal security audit. Dependencies and future expanded source constructs require renewed review.
